---
title: "Robyn"
---

`chameleon_rs.robyn` renders templates from [Robyn](https://robyn.tech) route handlers. It has
chameleon-robyn's API, so moving an app over is an import change, or no change at all with
`chameleon_rs.compat.install()` (which makes `import chameleon_robyn` give this module).

`import chameleon_rs` doesn't import Robyn. Only `import chameleon_rs.robyn` does. There is
nothing extra to install: it uses the Robyn your app already has.

::: {.callout-note}
## Python versions

Robyn publishes wheels for CPython 3.10 to 3.14 only (no 3.15 and no free-threaded build yet),
so `chameleon_rs.robyn` works wherever Robyn installs. The examples on this page are not run
when the docs are built, as the other framework pages are.
:::

## A first handler

```python
from robyn import Robyn

import chameleon_rs.robyn as chameleon

app = Robyn(__file__)
chameleon.configure(template_folder='templates', auto_reload=dev_mode, app=app)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def index(query_params):
    videos = ['intro', 'partials', 'async']
    return {'message': 'Hello', 'videos': videos[: int(query_params.get('limit', '2'))]}


app.start(port=8080)
```

The handler returns the template's model, and `@template` renders it into a `robyn.Response`
with `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`. The decorated handler keeps its signature, so
Robyn passes it the same request parts (`request`, `query_params`, path parameters, ...) as
without `@template`.

`configure()` here is the same call as `chameleon_rs.configure()`, so it also tells
`render_partial` where templates live. `app=` turns on the decorator-order check below.
`global_init(template_folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True, restricted_namespace=True)`
is chameleon-robyn's call and still works.

## Decorator order

`@template` goes below the route decorator. Written above it, Robyn registers the bare
handler, the template never renders and the route quietly returns the handler's dict as JSON.
An app given to `configure(..., app=app)` checks this when it starts:

```python
@chameleon.template('home/about.pt')   # wrong: above the route
@app.get('/about')
def about():
    return {'message': 'About'}


app.start(port=8080)
# chameleon_rs.web.DecoratorOrderError: @template must be placed below the route decorator
# (@app.get, @app.post, @router.get, app.add_route, ...) on about() at app.py:12
# (route GET /about): the route was registered with the undecorated view, so its template
# never renders. Put the route decorator first (outermost) and @template under it.
```

The check runs in `app.start()`, in the main process before the server starts, so a
misordered app fails to start. Robyn's own startup hook was not used: an app has one startup
handler (a second `startup_handler` replaces the first) and Robyn runs it inside each server
process. Robyn's in-process test client (`robyn.testing.TestClient(app)`) never calls
`start()`, so the check also runs whenever the app's route table is read with routes added
since the last check, which the test client does when it is built: a misordered app fails
there too. Reading the table early (a route listing built at import time) does not end the
check: routes added afterwards are checked at the next read and in `start()`. Once `start()`
passed the check, both hooks remove themselves.

Routes of a `SubRouter` included with `app.include_router(...)` are checked with the app.
`chameleon.check_views(app)` (or a `SubRouter`) runs the same check on demand. A
function registered raw on purpose (JSON on one route) and also decorated on another route is
not flagged. One pattern can't be told from the mistake: a function routed raw on this app
whose `@template` wrapper is used somewhere else (called from another handler, or routed on
another app). For such an app, pass `check_order=False` to `configure()` and keep the check in
a test with `chameleon.check_views(app, ignore=[that_function])`.

## Sync and async handlers

- An `async def` handler renders its page with `render_async` on Robyn's event loop. A model
  value that is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future) is awaited where the template uses it,
  so a slow query can be handed to the template unawaited, and other requests keep being served
  while it waits.
- A plain `def` handler renders with `render()` where Robyn runs it: on its Rust worker
  thread, not on the event loop and not in a thread pool. While it renders, that worker (one per
  process by default) handles nothing else, as with chameleon-robyn.

`@template(..., concurrent=True)` renders `render_partial(...)` calls with awaitable arguments
concurrently; `@template(..., offload=True)` (experimental) renders in a worker thread. Both
apply to `async def` handlers only.

## What a handler can return

- **A model:** a `dict`, any other mapping, a dataclass instance (its fields, shallowly) or a
  Pydantic model (anything with a callable `model_dump()`).
- **A response:** a `robyn.Response` passes through unchanged (redirects, custom errors).

Anything else raises `chameleon_rs.robyn.ChameleonRobynException`.

A `__response_callback__` in the model is not a template variable: it is called with the
response before it is returned, to set cookies or headers. The handler's dict is not changed,
so a shared or module-level model keeps working.

```python
def remember(response):
    response.set_cookie('session', session_id)

@app.post('/login')
@chameleon.template('account/welcome.pt')
def login(request):
    return {'user': user, '__response_callback__': remember}
```

## The `@template` decorator

```python
@chameleon.template('home/index.pt')                       # a template path
@chameleon.template('feed.pt', 'application/xml')          # content_type=, or mimetype=
@chameleon.template('home/created.pt', status_code=201)
@chameleon.template                                        # no arguments
```

With no path, it renders `{module}/{function}.html`, where `{module}` is the last part of the
handler's module name; if there's no `.html` file in the template folder, it uses
`{module}/{function}.pt`. As in chameleon-robyn, the choice is made at the first request, once
a template folder is configured, so handlers can be decorated at import time and
`global_init()` called later from `main()`.

## Error pages

Inside a decorated handler, `not_found()` and `error()` stop the handler and render an error
page as `text/html`. The template gets `message` (`'The URL resulted in a 404 response.'` or
`'The URL resulted in an error.'`) and the data passed:

```python
@app.get('/videos/:name')
@chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def video(name):
    if name not in videos:
        chameleon.not_found(name=name)   # renders errors/404.pt with status 404
    return {'message': name, 'videos': [name]}
```

- `not_found(template_file='errors/404.pt', **data)` renders the page with status 404
  (`four04template_file=` is chameleon-robyn's name for the template).
- `error(template_file, status_code=500, **data)` renders any error page.
- `generic_error(template_file, status_code, template_data)` is fastapi-chameleon's name and
  signature for `error()`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Template names come from your code

The names given to `@template`, `render()`, `response()`, `not_found()` / `error()`,
`ChameleonTemplate.render_template()` and `render_partial()` are looked up as the original
libraries look them up, which allows `..` and absolute paths. Write them in your code; never
build one from a request (a path or query parameter, a header).
:::

## Rendering without the decorator

```python
html = chameleon.render('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)        # a str
html = await chameleon.render_async('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)
resp = chameleon.response('feed.pt', 'application/xml', items=items)
resp = await chameleon.response_async('feed.pt', status_code=201, items=items)
```

Both raise `ChameleonRobynException` if nothing has been configured.

## Robyn's template interface

`ChameleonTemplate` implements Robyn's `TemplateInterface`, as its `JinjaTemplate` does. It
has a loader of its own and needs no `configure()`:

```python
from chameleon_rs.robyn import ChameleonTemplate

templates = ChameleonTemplate('templates', auto_reload=dev_mode)


@app.get('/about')
async def about():
    return await templates.render_template_async('home/about.pt', message='About')
```

`render_template(name, **data)` returns a 200 `robyn.Response`; `render_template_async` is
its coroutine. `robyn.templating.render(name, template_engine=ChameleonTemplate, ...)` works
too, and type-checks there. (At runtime `ChameleonTemplate` follows Robyn's interface without
subclassing its abstract class, which would import Jinja2, as chameleon-robyn does.)

## Coming from chameleon-robyn

| chameleon-robyn | chameleon-rs |
|---|---|
| `global_init(folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True, restricted_namespace=True)` | Still works, and takes `app=`. It configures the handlers only, as before, and ignores a second call. `configure()` sets handlers and partials together, and every call applies. |
| `@template(file, content_type, status_code)`, `render`, `response`, `not_found`, `clear`, `ChameleonTemplate` | Same. `@template` also takes `mimetype=`, `concurrent=` and `offload=`; `not_found` also takes `template_file=` and template data. |
| — | `error()`, `generic_error()`, `render_async()`, `response_async()`, `ChameleonTemplate.render_template_async()`, `check_views()`. |
| `ChameleonRobynException`, `ChameleonRobynNotFoundException` | Same names, now subclasses of `chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError` and `NotFound`. |
| Handlers return a `dict` | Also mappings, dataclasses and Pydantic models. |
| Async handlers render synchronously | They render with `render_async`; an awaitable model value is awaited where the template uses it. |

Settings are process-wide: a Robyn handler has no app to find settings of its own in.
